10815-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson compiled the Messages and Papers of the Presidents by authority of Congress, and this fourth volume covers March 4, 1841, to March 4, 1849. It holds the terms of Harrison and Tyler and the term of James K. Polk. The death of President Harrison, the first time a vice-president succeeded under the Constitution, opens the period, with papers on his death included.

Tyler's vetoes, including two against bills chartering a national bank, appear among the documents. The volume is a primary source for the age of expansion and party strife. Readers and researchers get the presidents' own words, in official form, for eight crowded years.
10858-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's compilation turns to Andrew Jackson in this volume, covering his first term from March 4, 1829, to March 4, 1833. A short life opens it: Jackson was born in the Waxhaw settlement in 1767, son of an Irish immigrant who died the year he was born. Captured by the British in 1781 and wounded for refusing to clean an officer's boots, he studied law at Salisbury and moved to Nashville.

The volume then prints Jackson's messages and proclamations, the record of a turbulent presidency. Richardson's series preserves the official papers in order. Readers get Jackson's public voice, framed by the hard youth that made him.
10879-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson gathered the official papers of John Quincy Adams in this volume of his presidential series. A short life sketch opens the book, tracing Adams from his boyhood travels in Europe through Harvard, the law, and diplomatic posts in Holland, Prussia, and Russia. It then presents the documents of his presidency, in the order the administration issued them.

Readers get the presidency in its own words: messages to Congress, proclamations, and papers on foreign affairs and public finance. The volume shows how Adams explained his policies and answered Congress, and it preserves the record of a single administration for later study. Students of the early republic can follow debates over trade, debt, and the nation's place abroad without relying on secondhand summaries.
10893-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's series reaches Thomas Jefferson in this volume, covering March 1801 to March 1809. A life sketch follows Jefferson from Shadwell, Virginia, through William and Mary, the law, and the Virginia legislature to the Continental Congress, where he drafted the Declaration of Independence. Diplomatic service in France and the office of Secretary of State come before the presidency.

Jefferson's own papers follow: messages to Congress, proclamations, and documents on the Louisiana Purchase, relations with France and Spain, and disputes over trade and western boundaries. The volume lets readers hear the third president explain his decisions in formal, public language. It serves as a primary source for the politics and diplomacy of the early republic.
10894-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's compilation of presidential messages and papers gives John Adams his own section, covering March 4, 1797, to March 4, 1801. A short life opens it: Adams was born near Boston in 1735, entered Harvard in 1751, studied law, taught at Worcester, and married Abigail Smith in 1764. He rose at the Boston bar before the Revolution.

The volume then prints Adams's messages, addresses, and proclamations as president, in official form. Richardson's series aimed to put every president's public papers within reach. Readers and researchers get Adams in his own words, with a compact life to set them in context.
10895-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James Madison takes centre stage in this volume of Richardson's presidential papers, covering March 1809 to March 1817. A sketch traces Madison from Virginia boyhood and Princeton through the Continental Congress and the 1787 Constitutional Convention, where he played a leading part. Service in the House and as Jefferson's Secretary of State preceded his own two terms.

Madison's messages then speak for themselves, including his war messages against Britain and his complaints about British commanders using Native allies in battle. Trade, finance, and the defence of the young republic run through the papers. Readers can follow a president guiding the nation through the War of 1812 and into peace, in documents written for Congress and the public.
10919-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's second volume of his compilation of presidential messages and papers, dated 1897, followed a first volume welcomed by Congress and the press. Congress ordered fifteen thousand additional copies of the whole publication after the first volume appeared about May 1, 1896. This volume adds a steel engraving of the Treasury building, with more public buildings to follow.

The work prints annual, special, and veto messages, inaugural addresses, proclamations, and other papers from the chief magistrate. Richardson's aim was a complete, official record for citizens and scholars. Readers get a stately source book of the early presidency, in its original form.
10951-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
Volume five, part one, of James D. Richardson's compilation covers twelve years before the Civil War, from the Taylor-Fillmore administration through Pierce and Buchanan to March 1861. Richardson's preface names the great issues of the period: the Compromise of 1850, the admission of California, Minnesota, Oregon, and Kansas, the Gadsden Purchase, Kansas-Nebraska, the Dred Scott decision.

Veto messages feature strongly, as Pierce rejects land grants and internal improvements and Buchanan rejects homestead and agricultural bills. Buchanan's protests against a House inquiry into his conduct also appear. The volume is a primary source for the sectional crisis, showing presidents defending their policies in public while the Union slid toward war.
11021-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James Buchanan's presidency fills this volume of Richardson's compilation, covering March 1857 to March 1861. A sketch traces Buchanan from Mercersburg, Pennsylvania, where he was born in 1791 to a Scotch-Irish farmer, through Dickinson College and Lancaster law practice, to the state legislature, ten years in Congress.

Buchanan's papers then record the sectional crisis: Kansas, slavery, secession, and the defence of the Union as states left after Lincoln's election. Orders for half-hour guns and flags at half-staff after a statesman's death show the formal side of the office. The volume is a primary source for the last months of peace, written in the language of a president trying to hold a breaking nation together.
11034-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
Martin Van Buren's presidency fills this volume of James D. Richardson's compilation, covering March 1837 to March 1841. A sketch traces Van Buren from Kinderhook, New York, where he was born in 1782, through law study at fourteen, the New York bar, and state politics as a Jeffersonian.

Van Buren's papers follow, including messages on Indian treaties, naval surveys, and lighthouse sites, sent to the Senate and to Speaker James K. Polk. The documents show a president managing finance, expansion, and federal administration after the Panic of 1837. Readers get the administration in its official voice, useful for studying Jacksonian politics and the presidency between Jackson and Tyler.
11125-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson compiled this volume of the messages and papers of the presidents, covering Franklin Pierce, March 4, 1853, to March 4, 1857. Pierce was born in Hillsboro, New Hampshire, on November 23, 1804, fourth son of Benjamin Pierce, a Revolutionary soldier who became governor of New Hampshire. Franklin studied at Hancock, Francestown, and Exeter, then at Bowdoin College, where his mates included Longfellow and Hawthorne.

Pierce graduated in 1824, studied law, served in the New Hampshire legislature as speaker, then in Congress, where his first important speech urged economy and watchfulness against fraud. Later pages discuss claims against the government, noting that no president had deemed them worthy of recommendation to Congress. The volume preserves Pierce's messages and papers as a reference for historians of the 1850s.
1119-king-henry-v:
Henry V, the wild prince turned king, claims France, crosses the Channel, and wins the impossible victory of Agincourt against a far larger French army. William Shakespeare's history play follows him from the London taverns of his youth to the muddy field, with the Chorus begging the audience to imagine the rest.

Henry woos the French princess, rallies his men with the St. Crispin's Day speech, and proves a king of wit, nerve, and ruthlessness. The play's patriotism and its doubts sit side by side. It remains the great English war play, rousing and troubling at once.
11202-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's third volume of presidential papers, published by authority of Congress with copyright 1897, covers Andrew Jackson's second term and Martin Van Buren's presidency. It prints Jackson's reasons for removing deposits from the United States Bank, his Farewell Address. Papers on the gold-silver ratio, alongside Van Buren's message urging an independent treasury, the divorce of bank and state.

A dispute with Britain over the northeastern boundary also appears among Van Buren's papers. Richardson's preface notes the surprise that eight years could fill a volume, but argues the material matches earlier volumes in interest. For researchers, the book is a primary source for Jacksonian finance and diplomacy.
11230-macmillan-s-reading-books-book-v:
Macmillan's Reading Book V, for Standard V under the English and Scotch education codes, provided graded prose and poetry for schoolchildren facing state inspection. Pupils were expected to read with expression, recite at least seventy-five lines of poetry, and parse simple sentences, with three hundred lines required for the Scotch code's second-year literature subject. A preface explains the series as a systematic course matched to each standard.

The selections mix old ballads with standard authors, chosen so teachers could test meaning, allusion, and derivation. The book's interest now is educational: it shows what Victorian and Edwardian schools counted as literacy. Its apparatus of codes and grants reveals a classroom governed by examination.
11239-the-life-and-adventures-of-robinso:
This 1812 London edition prints Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe in two volumes, preceded by a life of Defoe tracing him from a London butcher's son to pamphleteer and author. Crusoe's own narrative follows: shipwreck, solitude on an island, and slow mastery of farming, building, and survival over many years. Friday's arrival later turns the solitary tale into a story of companionship and rule.

The edition matters because it shows Crusoe as early nineteenth-century readers met him, framed as a true account written by himself. Its long life testifies to the book's grip on ideas of self-reliance and empire. Modern readers can follow both the adventure and the period attitudes embedded in it.
11314-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's first volume of presidential papers, issued in 1897 under the Joint Committee on Printing, opens the series with a preface defending the project. presidential messages, vetoes, orders, and addresses are among the most valuable parts of American public writing. Richardson gathered nearly all proclamations, addresses, messages, and letters to Congress, leaving out only nominations, treaty notes, and department reports.

The volume sets the pattern for the series, making founding-era papers handy in compact form for lawmakers, students, and scholars. Its claim is practical: no earlier government publication had collected these papers together. Readers still use Richardson's book as a gateway to early presidential writing.
12318-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson compiled this eighth volume of presidential messages and papers in 1897, covering March 4, 1881, to March 4, 1889. Richardson, a Tennessee representative, gathered official documents for Congress and the public.

The volume spans the Garfield-Arthur term and Cleveland first term. It opens with Garfield assassination: the president shot at a station and carried to a private room. He was later removed to the Executive Mansion, while Vice President Arthur succeeded him, the fourth such succession in American history. Later papers cover tariffs, civil service, and foreign affairs. The book is a reference work, valuable for the documents themselves rather than for narrative.
12462-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's sixth volume of presidential papers covers March 1861 to March 1869, the administrations of Lincoln and Johnson. Richardson notes that no period since the Revolution holds so many events of surpassing importance. Lincoln's years were given to civil war, Johnson's to restoring peace and the Union as it had stood.

Messages, proclamations and state papers follow in order, letting readers trace war, emancipation, reconstruction and impeachment in official words. Richardson calls Lincoln a kind-hearted humanitarian who loved peace, yet had to wage a bloody conflict. The volume is a primary source for the Civil War era, valuable precisely because it lets documents speak before historians summarise them.
12463-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's compilation gathers the messages and papers of James K. Polk, president from March 1845 to March 1849. A short life opens the volume, tracing Polk from his birth in North Carolina in 1795, through a Tennessee farm boyhood, to the White House, before the documents themselves begin.

Inside are presidential messages to Congress, proclamations and state papers of an administration that annexed Texas, settled Oregon and fought Mexico. Read in sequence they show how Polk stated his aims, defended his acts and managed a fast-expanding nation. The volume serves as a primary source, letting readers hear a presidency in its own official voice rather than through later summary.
12464-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's volume on John Tyler covers April 1841 to March 1845, opening with Tyler's life. Born at Greenway, Virginia, in 1790, son of a governor, Tyler graduated from William and Mary in 1807, loved history and music, played the violin, and entered the bar in 1809. Election to the legislature followed in 1811.

As president after Harrison's death, Tyler faced annexation, tariff and party quarrels, and his messages and papers record those struggles in official form. Richardson's compilation lets readers follow a much-criticised presidency through its own documents. The volume serves students of the 1840s, when Texas, Oregon and party division shaped the road to later crisis.
12754-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's volume on Chester A. Arthur covers September 1881 to March 1885, opening with Arthur's life. Born in Fairfield, Vermont, on 5 October 1830, Arthur was eldest son of Reverend William Arthur, a Baptist minister born in Ireland, and Malvina Stone. He prepared at Union Village and Schenectady, entering Union College as a sophomore in 1845.

Teaching terms at Schaghticoke and Psi Upsilon membership follow. He was elected as one of six in a class of one hundred to Phi Beta Kappa, for high scholarship. As president after Garfield's death, Arthur faced civil service reform, tariffs and party strife, recorded in messages and papers. The volume offers a primary source for a quiet, surprising presidency.
12755-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
Compiled by James D. Richardson, this volume gathers the public papers of President Andrew Johnson, from April 1865 to March 1869. A short life opens the book. Johnson was born poor in Raleigh in 1808, apprenticed to a tailor at ten, taught the alphabet by a fellow worker, and helped to write by his wife Eliza. Office by office, Johnson rose from alderman to president.

The bulk is official text: messages to Senate and House, reports, vetoes, and notes on treaties, including a Hawaiian reciprocity treaty in 1867. Readers get Johnson's Reconstruction years in his own formal voice. The volume serves historians who need the primary record, not a retelling.
13012-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's seventh volume of presidential papers covers Ulysses S. Grant's eight years and Rutherford B. Hayes's four, from March 1869 to March 1881. The prefatory note calls Grant's election a republic's gratitude to a successful soldier, who would never have risen without the Civil War. Restoration of southern states and reunion of the Union mark the period.

Grant's messages press civil service reform, asking Congress for strength to carry out a commission's rules, set to take effect on January 1, 1872. The volume gives the primary record of Reconstruction's close. Historians will find here Grant and Hayes in their own formal words.
13021-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's compilation gathers the official papers of President Rutherford B. Hayes, who served from March 4, 1877, to March 4, 1881. A short life opens the volume: Hayes was born in Delaware, Ohio, in 1822, studied Latin and Greek, entered Kenyon College in 1838, and won praise as a debater. The main text then gives his messages to Congress in full.

Hayes writes on yellow fever and the need for national sanitary control, sending tents and rations worth about twenty-five thousand dollars to stricken towns. He returns again and again to the franchise, urging full and safe voting for all citizens. The volume is a primary source for Reconstruction's end, in the president's own formal words.
13235-in-the-ranks-of-the-c-i-v:
Driver Erskine Childers, a clerk in the House of Commons, published In the Ranks of the C.I.V. in 1900 as a diary of service with the City Imperial Volunteers battery in South Africa. Childers dedicates it to his friend and comrade Gunner Basil Williams. Chapters run from the Montfort and Cape Town through Bloemfontein, Lindley, Bethlehem, and on to Pretoria.

Childers records stable duty, icy washes from an ammunition box, frost at night, and snug lairs under quartermaster's stores. Shifting camp a mile brings grumbles, as fuel and meal must be decanted into tins and wallets. The diary is a vivid, unheroic record of volunteer war: marching, waiting, and small comforts kept with care.
13617-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson compiles the messages and papers of the presidents in volume nine, published by authority of Congress in 1902, covering Benjamin Harrison and Grover Cleveland's second term to March 4, 1897. Richardson, a Tennessee representative, began the work in April 1895 after the Fifty-third Congress and gave it his whole time outside official duties.

Sugar beet cultivation, civil service law, and the transfer of sugar supervision to the Department of Agriculture fill Harrison and Cleveland papers. Greer County, occupied by Texas citizens on more than a million and a half acres, is claimed by Choctaws and Chickasaws, with the United States suing to declare it Indian country. The volume is a documentary record of two administrations.
14137-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
This volume gathers the public papers of Grover Cleveland's second term, from March 1893 to March 1897. Inaugural and annual messages lead, with Cleveland pledging devotion to the people's welfare and warning against tendencies that menace sound government. Vetoes, proclamations, and messages to Congress follow in order, forming a record of a presidency rather than a narrative life.

Foreign and domestic business fills the pages. Cleveland sends condolences on President Carnot's death, protests a revived German ban on American cattle over Texas fever, and disputes a sugar duty aimed at bounty-paying countries. At home he reports on Armenian-born naturalized citizens in Turkey and urges payment for rail transport of colonists returned from Mexico to Alabama. Historians value the set as a primary source, dense but exact.
14417-the-agamemnon-of-aeschylus-transla:
Gilbert Murray, Regius Professor of Greek at Oxford, rendered Aeschylus's Agamemnon into English rhyming verse, with explanatory notes, in this popular edition. The play, first performed in Athens in 458 BC, opens the Oresteia trilogy.

A watchman waits for the beacon announcing Troy's fall, and King Agamemnon returns home to his wife Clytemnestra, his captive prophetess Cassandra, and a murderous welcome. The chorus of Argive elders meditates on pride, guilt, and fate. Murray's verse keeps the drama singable, and his notes guide readers through the Greek stagecraft. Later translations owe much to his clear, musical line.
1521-king-henry-v:
Shakespeare's Henry V follows the former Prince Hal, now king, from a London council chamber to the fields of Agincourt. A chorus begs the audience to imagine great armies with few players, and the play moves from Harfleur's siege to the eve of battle, where Henry walks disguised among his men.

The St Crispin's Day speech and the victory over a larger French force crown a king who has learned both war and mercy. The play is Shakespeare's most stirring history. It celebrates leadership while letting the costs of war, in camp and court, show through the glory.
15863-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
A volume from the great compilation of presidential messages and papers, in the Richardson tradition. The volume opens with Grover Cleveland and his first term, March 1885 to March 1889. A short life of Cleveland fronts the papers, tracing his family from Moses Cleveland of Ipswich to his father, a Yale minister. Official texts follow in full.

Messages to Congress, proclamations, and executive orders show Cleveland at work: vetoes, civil service, and the tariff fight. The compilation's value lies in completeness, letting readers hear a president in his own words. For students of the Gilded Age, the volume gives the record straight, without later comment to soften it.
16415-tales-from-many-sources-vol-v:
This 1886 volume gathers seven tales first printed in magazines like Temple Bar and Belgravia. Juliana H. Ewing opens with Lob Lie-by-the-Fire, about a rough house elf who threshes corn by night for a bowl of cream. A balloon trip, a tale of Virginia, a numbered prisoner, and a Goneril story follow.

The mix is wide: folk fancy, modern life, and quiet social drama sit side by side. Each tale can be read alone, and the range shows what magazine fiction offered late Victorian readers. The Ewing opener is the gem, full of north-country charm, but the whole set rewards a reader who likes short stories with varied moods.
17845-salem-witchcraft-volumes-i-and-ii-:
Charles W. Upham wrote Salem Witchcraft, first printed in 1867 and reissued by Frederick Ungar in New York, joining volumes one and two in a single text. Upham, a Salem man and scholar, set out to give both the village story and a history of views on witchcraft.

Volume one covers Salem Village and the rise of witch belief, while volume two follows the trials at Salem Village itself, with a supplement and appendix. Maps, lists, and a general index aid the reader. Upham writes with care and moral force, and his work still stands as a classic, humane study of the 1692 delusion.
18524-a-dark-month-from-swinburne-s-coll:
Algernon Charles Swinburne's A Dark Month appears here as taken from volume five of his collected poetical works, published by William Heinemann in London in 1917. Volume five gathers Studies in Song, A Century of Roundels, Sonnets on English Dramatic Poets, and the Heptalogia, with other pieces. A Dark Month stands among the shorter poems of that set, first printed by Chatto in 1904.

The poem takes Victor Hugo's line as epigraph: la maison sans enfants, the house without children. That phrase sets the month's darkness: a house, a loss, and a season of grief. Swinburne writes in his musical, elegiac manner, with the sea and the year turning behind the personal sorrow. Readers get a short, somber lyric from a poet known for fire: a dark month, a childless house, and verse that holds grief in form.
20762-chancellorsville-and-gettysburg-ca:
Abner Doubleday fought at Gettysburg, and his campaign history speaks with a soldier's frankness. He warns that fresh events draw sharp fire from those who lived them. A bland tale that praises all and blames none, he says, would waste the war's hard lessons.

Chancellorsville and Gettysburg, two vast battles of 1863, fill this volume of the Campaigns of the Civil War set. Doubleday held ground at Gettysburg on the first day. His account weighs plans, ground, and command choices in plain terms. Readers get a Union view from a man who stood in the line himself.
2253-king-henry-v:
Henry V, once the wild Prince Hal, claims the French throne and leads a small English army to Agincourt. Shakespeare's history follows the king from the tennis-ball insult through the siege of Harfleur to the St Crispin's Day speech. The Chorus begs the audience to imagine vast battles on a bare stage. The victory comes at terrible cost.

Around the heroics, the play questions war itself: soldiers debate the king's responsibility the night before battle, and Falstaff's old friends die in its shadow. Henry's wooing of Katherine closes the action with humor and hope. It is both a patriotic pageant and a study of leadership.
22796-impressions-of-america-during-the-:
Tyrone Power wrote Impressions of America during the Years 1833, 1834, and 1835, a celebrated Irish actor's account of his American tours. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Power, grandfather of the later stage and film stars of his name, played to packed houses from New York to New Orleans and wrote down what he saw.

His aim, stated in the preface, is repayment. If he can dissipate one common error, he says, he will be content. Eradicating one vulgar prejudice, or kindling one kindly feeling, would do as well. Then he would have returned the high favor with which America repaid his efforts to please. The volumes that follow mix theater gossip with sharp notes on manners, politics, and slavery. Power's America is the young republic seen by a friendly, watchful guest.
23284-impressions-of-america-during-the-:
Impressions of America records a traveller's view of the United States in the years 1833, 1834, and 1835. Not every impression is of crowds or politics. One passage sits in the upper gallery of a house upon a cliff, watching the rising moon at work.

Moonlight throws a golden bridge across the water, from the far horizon to the beach below. Such a sight, the writer says, would be worth something in a poet's or painter's eyes. Readers get an early foreign account of America that mixes close observation of a young republic with outright wonder at its scenery.
24195-history-of-the-159th-regiment-n-y-:
This history of the 159th Regiment, New York State Volunteers, was compiled from the diary of Lieutenant Edward Duffy. It was published in New York in 1890, reprinted from the Hudson Gazette of 1865 in one hundred and fifty copies. In late October 1862, the 167th Regiment under Colonel Homer A. Nelson at Hudson joined with the 159th under Lieutenant-Colonel Edward L. Molineux at Brooklyn, keeping the 159th name with Nelson in command.

The regiment left Camp Kelly at Hudson on October 30 and sailed on the steamer Connecticut. It marched to Park Barracks in New York, and was mustered into United States service on November 1 by Lieutenant R. B. Smith. From Castle Garden it went by steamboat to Staten Island and Camp New Dorp. Readers get a Civil War regiment's record, kept close to a diary.
28050-women-as-sex-vendors-or-why-women-:
R. B. Tobias and Mary E. Marcy published Women as Sex Vendors, or Why Women Are Conservative, in Chicago with Charles H. Kerr and Company in 1918, subtitled a view of the economic status of woman. The book argues that women, as owners of a commodity vital to men's health and well-being, occupy a favored biologic and economic position.

Because the favored class rarely revolts against a system that advantages it, women have seldom been revolutionists, while a true revolutionist owns nothing to sell except his power to work. The socialist-feminist argument, blunt in its title, remains a provocative early statement on sex, economics, and conservatism.
29854-the-works-of-aphra-behn-volume-v:
Volume five of the works of Aphra Behn gathers her short fiction, with notes placed after each story in this text. The Epistle Dedicatory to Oroonoko, printed as an appendix in the book, stands just before the novel itself, as the editor intended. Cross-references from other volumes of the complete works follow the notes, and the New English Dictionary is now known as the Oxford English Dictionary.

Thirteen tales fill the volume, from The Adventure of the Black Lady and The Court of the King of Bantam to The Fair Jilt and The Unfortunate Happy Lady. Oroonoko, or The Royal Slave, stands at the heart of the set, with Agnes de Castro and The History of the Nun beside it. The Lucky Mistake, The Dumb Virgin, and The Wandering Beauty close the run. The book is a rich shelf of Restoration prose fiction.
29878-the-history-of-woman-suffrage-volu:
Ida Husted Harper edited volume five of The History of Woman Suffrage, covering 1900 to 1920, printed in 1922 for the National American Woman Suffrage Association. Its motto reads After Seventy Years Came the Victory. A frontispiece shows Dr. Anna Howard Shaw, vice-president-at-large of the association from 1892 to 1904 and president from 1904 to 1915. Copperplate and photogravure engravings illustrate the volume, the fifth of six.

Chapter one treats the founding of the National Association and its work for a federal amendment, state amendments, and other reforms. The annual convention at Minneapolis in 1901 and Mrs. Stanton's address on the church, the Bible, and woman suffrage follow. The volume carries the movement from the turn of the century to the vote itself, written by the women who led it, with documents close at hand.
31156-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Volume six, slice one of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica covers the alphabet from Châtelet to Chicago. Its article list runs from Chatham, Chatsworth, and Chattanooga through Chatterji, Bankim Chandra, Chatterton, Chaucer, and the Cherokee. It goes on to chess, chemistry, and the cheetah, with entries on places, people, arts, and sciences in between.

As a slice of the great 1910 reference work, the volume shows the Britannica's method at full stretch: concise, authoritative articles meant to answer a reader's question in a few pages. For modern users, it doubles as a snapshot of what the Edwardian world thought worth knowing, from French towns to American cities.
31771-si-klegg-book-1-his-transformation:
John McElroy's first Si Klegg book, in its second edition of 1910, follows Si's transformation from a raw recruit to a veteran. Its twenty-two chapters run from going to war and Si's complete equipment through the deadly bayonet, the old canteen, and the awful hardtack. Fat pork is described as indispensable body timber for patriotism.

Si is detailed as cook, joins the awkward squad, gets a letter, meets the doctors, straggles, handles mules, and at last comes under fire, fights, and captures a prisoner. Readers get the opening volume of a beloved Civil War comedy, built from sketches first published in The National Tribune.
32604-the-story-of-the-raising-and-organ:
Ellis Spear, a brevet brigadier general, tells how a volunteer regiment was raised and put in the field in 1862. Read before the Military Order of the Loyal Legion in 1903, his paper skips battles. Instead it explains the unglamorous start of soldiering.

Private men recruited at their own cost under the governor's writ, hoping for commissions in the companies they raised. Spear follows them into camp, where drill at first looks like a town meeting. He shows how raw men and green officers slowly learned to march, dress ranks, and parade.
6155-athens-its-rise-and-fall-book-v:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's fifth book runs from Cimon's death in 449 BC to Pericles's death in the third year of the Peloponnesian War, 429 BC. Thucydides, chosen by the aristocratic party to oppose Pericles, opens the book, with his policy, Pericles's munificence, the sacred war, and Coronea.

Revolt of Euboea and Megara, invasion and retreat of Peloponnesians, reduction of Euboea, punishment of Histiaea, and a thirty years' truce follow, with Thucydides ostracized. On Cimon's death the aristocrats needed a home leader, not a distant general, to meet Pericles in assembly and intrigue. This book alone is described here.
6261-the-weavers-a-tale-of-england-and-e:
A village lies in a valley once the bed of a great river, in days when Ireland, Wales, and Brittany were joined and the Thames flowed into the Seine. For generations it has lived serenely, never knowing turmoil. Three buildings stand out. A square red brick mansion sits behind a high wall. A low ivy covered house, once a monastery and called the Cloistered House, stands beside a plain wooden hall with heavy oak doors and diamond panes.

This opening part, Book One, follows David Claridge as the spirit moves him, through the gates of the world, banishment, and a call that pulls him from Hamley toward Egypt. His grandfather Luke watches forces stir in the boy that Claridge blood did not plant. Parker writes a quiet English valley first, so that the wider world, when it comes, breaks on a peace the reader has learned to love.
6262-the-weavers-a-tale-of-england-and-e:
Months later, a letter reaches David Claridge in Cairo from Faith Claridge in Hamley, asking if he still loves the village people who once gave him sour bread. She tells of Kimber, the man David struck at a public house, who followed to London the lass David kissed and begged her to marry him. Refused at first with anger, she promised an answer in three years if he stayed sober and hard working meanwhile.

This part of the novel, Book Two, widens David's way from Hamley to Cairo, through a compact, a letter, a night, and a woman, and on to a jehad and lions. Four people know a secret, a ropemaking man strikes, and the tale passes beyond the pale. Parker sets a Quaker village voice against Egyptian courts, where Nahoum rises and David's face, white at the palace, hides a deeper game.
6263-the-weavers-a-tale-of-england-and-e:
Faith raises her eyes from a paper and talks with Soolsby, who rests his chin on a chair he is caning and smiles with suppressed amusement. Three years have passed since a promise was made. Soolsby would drink no more until David's return, and Faith counts the time as an old memory, though she calls herself almost an old woman now. Soolsby answers that time is afraid of her and lets her be.

This part, Book Three, opens with Soolsby's hand upon the curtain and runs through debt and accounting, a woman of the crossroads, time the idol breaker, and sharper than a sword. Old antagonism flares again, one strong will resenting another, as if the world held no room for both. Parker writes Hamley waiting and Egypt working, with Faith at the centre, patient, watchful, and far from passive.
6264-the-weavers-a-tale-of-england-and-e:
Higli Pasha laughs to himself in a courtyard of Nahoum Pasha's palace, narghileh stem in mouth, waiting for its owner with hilarious patience. Years have changed him little since the expedition against southern tribes that followed David's appointment to office. Diaz died of a tarantula bite, Higli took a slight wound and retreated safely to Cairo, and of the old conspirators only Nahoum and Higli remain, never partners in any true sense.

This part, Book Four, turns Nahoum's screw, with a recoil, a move by Lacey, a struggle in the desert, forty stripes save one, and a dark indenture. Nahoum at last drops his mask, and Prince Kaid's dark face turns on old friends. Parker writes palace intrigue as a slow tightening, where laughter in a courtyard can sit beside ruin, and a man's past bargains return to claim him.
6265-the-weavers-a-tale-of-england-and-e:
A tenor voice rings out in an opera house, singing words about souls in purgatory and a plea not to be forgotten. The sound finds far recesses of feeling in its hearers. Women of poise and social fame drop their eyes to opera glasses and programmes, recalling first married days and seals of devotion long since lost with fresh desires. Young lovers, happy and defiant in each other, are suddenly arrested by a music that speaks of a tragic Italian tale.

This part, Book Five, runs from the flight of the wounded through a flying shuttle, Jasper Kimber speaking, and Faith journeying to London. A woman pauses, moves on with purpose, and finds an opened letter on the floor whose first words scorch her eyes. Parker writes opera night as a mirror, where art stirs private memory and a single letter can turn a life.
6266-the-weavers-a-tale-of-england-and-e:
Hylda wakes, as it were, upon a scene unchanged, brilliant and full of colour, a chaos of decoration and noisy streams of life. Craftsmen crowd dark bazaars, merchants haggle on benches, hawkers cry their wares, and a people live upon the streets while houses seem empty. Sais run before a Pasha's carriage, donkey boys shriek for the right of way, and camels force a calm passage through swirling crowds.

This closing part, Book Six, sends Hylda to seek Nahoum, then into the land of Shinar and onto the loom of destiny. Word comes up the Nile, a wounded Arab is carried in with blood on his face, and David's face clouds at news he should have had sooner. Parker ends his long tale of England and Egypt with a city in full noise and a reckoning that has travelled fifty years to arrive.
9598-criticism-part-4-from-the-works-of-:
Part four of Whittier's Criticism holds his essays on poems and poets, led by a review of Longfellow's Evangeline. Whittier hails it as an American poem at last, telling the sad exile of Acadian settlers from Minas Basin. He praises its pictures of farm life, Indian summer, and the Ohio and Mississippi rivers. The range runs from Nova Scotia to the Gulf of Mexico.

Other essays in the part take up mirth and medicine, fame and glory, fanaticism, and the poetry of the North. Whittier judges as a poet and a moralist at once. A reader gets a critic's view of his age's verse, warm toward Longfellow and sharp on what makes poetry last.
9760-leila-or-the-siege-of-granada-book-:
Book five of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Leila, or The Siege of Granada, opens with the great battle. Dawn breaks on a night of ruin, and the Moors on Granada's walls see Ferdinand's whole army marching to assault. Burned camp wrecks lie behind, while pennons wave and trumpets sound ahead. The Moors, hoping for a Christian retreat, fill with alarm.

King Boabdil, at the head of his guards, rallies his men as the assault breaks. Lytton stages the siege's climax with pageantry and dread. A reader gets the final battle book of a Granada romance, where a kingdom's fate hangs on one morning's fight.
a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-papers: William Henry Harrison and his successors fill this fourth volume compiled by James Daniel Richardson. The volume spans eight years from 1841 to 1849, covering Harrison, Tyler, and Polk. It opens with the first succession of a vice president after a president's death. Richardson presents the official record of a turbulent period in American history.
a-dark-month-from-swinburne-s-collected-: Algernon Charles Swinburne's fifth volume gathers studies in song, a century of roundels, and sonnets on English dramatic poets. The volume also includes the Heptalogia and other pieces from his middle period. A Dark Month stands among these collected poems of varied form and theme. Swinburne's rich music and classical learning run through the whole selection.
al-masudi-prairies-dor-meynard-vol-v:
The fifth tome of Barbier de Meynard's Les Prairies d'Or appeared in 1869, midway in the nine-tome French set. Its author, al-Masudi of Baghdad, finished the Muruj al-Dhahab, the Meadows of Gold and Mines of Gems, in the last years of his life. He had spent decades on the roads and seas of Asia and Africa.

Few medieval books hold so much. The science of the earth, the tales of ancient kings, and the ways of Hindus, Persians, and Franks all stand beside the chronicle of the caliphs. Al-Masudi wrote to teach and to delight at once. The French editors add notes on the hard names and places. This middle tome carries the reader deep into the whole.
athens-its-rise-and-fall-book-v:
Book V of Athens: Its Rise and Fall, by Edward Bulwer Lytton, covers a famous span. It runs from the death of Cimon in 449 BC. It ends with the death of Pericles in 429, in the Peloponnesian War's third year. The aristocratic party, Lytton begins, needed a new kind of leader after Cimon. No dazzling general absent on distant expeditions would do. They needed a statesman. He must meet Pericles in the assembly with equal civil experience and oratorical talent. Their choice fell on Thucydides, Cimon's brother in law.

His policy and Pericles' public munificence fill the first movement. A sacred war and revolts follow. The ostracism of Thucydides leaves Pericles supreme. The book closes over the plague years and the great man's death.
britannica-1911-alexius-v:
Alexius V held the eastern Roman throne only while Constantinople fought for its life. His full name ran Alexius Ducas Murtzuphlos, and he was kin to the imperial house of the Angeli. A rising inside the city raised him on 5 February 1204, as the Latins of the Fourth Crusade pressed their siege. The revolt had thrown down Isaac II and Alexius IV.

Defence of the city fell to Alexius, and he led it with great courage until, on 12 April, no hope remained. He then ran from the city. He sought to join Alexius III in a stand against the Latins, but the former emperor had him blinded instead. Crusaders caught him next and killed him by throwing him off the Pillar of Theodosius, as the slayer of Alexius IV.
britannica-1911-baldwin-v:
Baldwin V was the child king of Jerusalem from 1183 to 1186. He was the son of Sibylla, daughter of Amalric I, by her first husband, William of Montferrat. Too young to rule, he held the crown in name only, under the regency of Raymund of Tripoli.

The 1911 Britannica entry is very short, and it keeps to the bare facts of the reign. Two points stand out in it. Saladin was advancing against the kingdom from outside. At the same time, quarrels split the court at home, above all the strife between the government and Guy of Lusignan, Sibylla's second husband.
britannica-1911-frederick-v:
Frederick V (1596-1632), elector palatine of the Rhine and king of Bohemia, was born at Amberg on 26 August 1596, son of Frederick IV. He became elector in 1610 under a guardian, came of age in 1614, and in 1613 had married Elizabeth, daughter of James I of England. He headed the Evangelical Union his father had founded.

In August 1619 the Bohemian estates deposed Ferdinand and chose Frederick as king, and he was crowned at Prague on 4 November. Four days later his forces were routed at the White Hill by Tilly, and the short reign ended. Mocked as the Winter King, he fled to the Netherlands, and in 1623 his electorate passed to Maximilian of Bavaria. He died at Mainz in 1632. His son Charles Louis regained the Palatinate in 1648, and his daughter Sophia was mother of George I.
britannica-1911-john-vi-or-v:
John VI or V (c. 1292–1383), surnamed Cantacuzene, was East Roman emperor, born at Constantinople and linked to the house of Palaeologus through his mother. Under Andronicus III he held the chief conduct of affairs from 1328. When the emperor died in 1341, Cantacuzene was left regent for the boy John Palaeologus.

Suspected by the empress and fought by a strong court party, he had himself crowned emperor at Didymoteichos. Six years of civil war followed, and both sides called in Serbs, Turks, and hired troops. With Turkish aid he entered Constantinople in 1347 and became joint emperor. Wars with Genoa and Serbia strained the shrunken empire. The Turks made their first lasting foothold in Europe at Callipolis in 1354. Late that year John Palaeologus retook the capital. Cantacuzene withdrew to a monastery, took the name Joasaph Christodulus, and wrote a history of 1320 to 1356 that defends his own acts.
britannica-1911-ladislaus-v:
Ladislaus V (1440–1457), king of Hungary and Bohemia, was the son of Albert of Hungary and Elizabeth, daughter of the emperor Sigismund. He was born at Komárom on the 22nd of February 1440, four months after his father's death — hence Ladislaus Posthumus. His mother had the holy crown stolen from its guardians at Visegrad and the infant crowned at Székesfehérvár on the 15th of May 1440. She then placed him under his uncle, the emperor Frederick III.

When Wladislaus III died in 1444 the Hungarian estates elected Ladislaus, but Frederick gave up the child and the crown only in 1452. The boy then passed to Ulrich Cillei, who filled him with hatred of the Hunyadis. He was crowned king of Bohemia on the 28th of October 1453. Careless of the Turkish danger, he hampered Hunyadi's plans and fled the country at the news of the siege of Belgrade.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-v:
Alexander V, born Pietro Philarghi about 1339 on Crete, was elected pope on 26 June 1409 and died at Bologna on 3 May 1410. Homeless and begging in a Cretan city, with neither parents nor relations known, he found a patron in a discerning Capuchin friar. The friar gave him an elementary education and guided him into the Franciscan order. At Paris he shone as professor, preacher, and writer, and wrote a commentary on the Sentences of Peter Lombard.

Returning to Italy, Philarghi served the Duke of Milan as tutor and ambassador. He rose through Piacenza, Vicenza, and Navoya to Archbishop of Milan in 1402, and became cardinal in 1405 and papal legate to Lombardy. He championed a council to end the Great Schism, and the cardinals chose him unanimously to fill the papal chair, presumably vacant. His ten-month pontificate was spent in failed efforts to reach Rome, then held by King Ladislas of Naples.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boniface-v:
Boniface V, a Neapolitan pope from 619 to 625, is remembered as the mildest of men, devoted above all to his clergy. He followed Deusdedit after the see stood empty for more than a year, and was consecrated on 23 December 619. Before his consecration, Italy had been shaken by the revolt of Eleutherius, exarch of Ravenna, who was slain by his own troops before reaching Rome.

The Liber Pontificalis credits him with rules on sanctuary rights, wills, and the duties of acolytes, who could not displace deacons at baptism in the Lateran. He completed and consecrated the cemetery of Saint Nicomedes. Bede records his affectionate letters to England, urging King Edwin of Northumbria toward the faith and Queen Ethelberga to work for her husband's conversion. He was buried in Saint Peter's on 25 October 625.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-emperor-charl:
Charles V, also Charles I of Spain, was the Habsburg ruler over whom the sun was said never to set, born at Ghent in 1500 and dead at Yuste in 1558. Son of Philip of Burgundy and Joanna, daughter of Ferdinand and Isabella, he inherited Burgundy in 1506. His aunt Margaret of Austria held the regency while he was a minor. Adrian of Utrecht, his teacher at Louvain, left a deep mark on his mind.

Declared of age in January 1515, he sought peace with France through the treaties of Paris in 1515 and Noyon in 1516. On Ferdinand of Aragon's death in 1516 he claimed Spain, took the title King of Castile, and reached Spain in the autumn of 1517, despite a popular brother Ferdinand. Power left to Burgundian favourites, above all Chievres, provoked the rising of the Comunidades. Later parts follow his election as emperor, his long wars, and his abdication at Yuste.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-felix-v:
Felix V was the antipope elected by the Council of Basle. Born Amadeus VIII of Savoy in 1383, he had retired to a semi-monastic life at Ripaille. The council, having deposed Eugene IV, chose the rich and powerful duke in 1439. He accepted in 1440 and was solemnly crowned at Basle that July.

Felix found recognition only in Savoy, Switzerland, and a few German lands. Many named cardinals refused the dignity he offered them. He quarrelled with Basle over revenues and rights for several years. In 1449 he submitted to Nicholas V and became Cardinal of St Sabina.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-v:
Henry V, German king and Roman emperor, was born in 1081 as son of Henry IV and died at Utrecht in 1125. Described as crafty, sullen, and harsh, he nevertheless defended crown rights with prudence and energy. He took the throne by a compact with the papacy and the princes, his father's bitterest opponents. Yet at once he adopted his father's policy, refusing above all to surrender investiture, the royal right over the German Church.

In 1110 Henry marched to Rome for his imperial coronation. There Paschal II proposed that bishops surrender all worldly possessions in return for the king abandoning investiture. The German princes rejected the scheme, Henry seized the pope and forced his demands, and excommunications followed. Defeated in Saxony in 1115 and crowned emperor at St. Peter's in 1117, he finally reached the Concordat of Worms in 1122, distinguishing ecclesiastical office from temporal possessions and ending the great investiture controversy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-adrian-v:
Pope Adrian V, Genoa-born Ottobuono Fieschi, nephew of Innocent IV, held the papacy only briefly in 1276. Viterbo elected him 12 July 1276. While still Cardinal Fieschi he had worked to mend relations in England between Henry III and the barons in revolt.

Once pope he cancelled Gregory X's strict conclave rules, but death on 18 August cut short his plan to replace them with gentler ones. He survived barely long enough, the entry says, to sense the weight of the papal mantle. Dante gives him a memorable dialogue in Purgatory, canto nineteen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-benedict:
Pope Benedict V, birth date unknown, died 4 July 965. Romans chose him pope in May 964 at a perilous moment. Otto I had deposed the unworthy John XII by force and set up his own man, Leo VIII. At their first chance the Romans threw Leo out, and when John XII died 14 May 964 they chose Cardinal-Deacon Benedict, famed for learning as Grammaticus.

Otto raged, marched on Rome, seized Benedict, and closed his pontificate 23 June 964. More likely Benedict was stripped of office by force than that he freely called himself an intruder. Having restored Leo, Otto took Benedict to Germany. Adaldag, Archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen, treated him with great kindness, and some German clergy still honoured him as pope. His body, first laid at Hamburg, later moved to Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-bl-urban:
Pope Blessed Urban V, born Guillaume de Grimoard at Grisac in Languedoc in 1310, reigned from 1362 to 1370 from Avignon. Educated at Montpellier and Toulouse, he became a Benedictine monk at Chirac. He was professed at Saint Victor in Marseilles, whose love for his order he kept even as pope, still wearing its habit. He took his doctorate in 1342 and became one of the greatest canonists of his day.

He taught canon law at Montpellier, Toulouse, Paris, and Avignon. He served as vicar-general of Clermont and Uzès, then became abbot of Saint Germain d'Auxerre's priory and of Saint Victor in 1361. His diplomatic missions to Milan, Italy, and Naples marked him out. The cardinals, deadlocked by jealousy, chose this non-cardinal for virtue, learning, and practical skill. He was consecrated on 6 November 1362, taking the name Urban because, as he said, all earlier Urbans had been saints.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-celestin:
Pope Celestine V, born Pietro di Murrone in 1215 in the Neapolitan province of Molise, was the hermit-pope who abdicated after five months. He became a Benedictine at seventeen and was ordained at Rome, then sought solitude on Monte Morone and the wilder Majella, modelling himself on the Baptist. His hair-shirt was knotted, an iron chain ringed his wasted frame, and he fasted daily except Sunday, keeping four Lents a year, three on bread and water.

Kindred spirits gathered around him until thirty-six monasteries with six hundred religious bore his name, approved as Celestines by Urban IV in 1264. In July 1294 his solitude was broken by election at Perugia, coronation at Aquila on 29 August, and abdication at Naples on 13 December. He died a prisoner in the castle of Fumone on 19 May 1296, after Boniface VIII dissolved the Spiritual Franciscans who had used his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-clement-:
Pope Clement V, born Bertrand de Got at Villandraut in Gascony in 1264, was elected on 5 June 1305 after an eleven-month conclave split between French and Italian cardinals. Ten of fifteen cardinals, mostly Italian, chose him. Villani's tale of a secret bargain with Philip the Fair in the forest of Saint-Jean-d'Angély is, the entry insists, quite unhistorical, though some understanding with the French king is likely.

As Archbishop of Bordeaux he was a subject of England's king yet a lifelong friend of Philip, while staying faithful to Boniface VIII. The cardinals begged him to come to Perugia and Rome for coronation, but he summoned them to Lyons, where he was crowned on 14 November 1305 before Philip in great pomp. A falling wall threw him from his horse in the procession, killing a brother and the aged Cardinal Orsini and losing the tiara's great carbuncle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-gregory-:
Pope Gregory V, born Bruno about 970, was the first German pope, consecrated on 3 May 996. On John XV's death the Romans asked Otto III to name his choice, and Otto named his chaplain and kinsman Bruno, son of Duke Otto of Carinthia and Judith. Already distinguished for learning, above all for the dialects that would grow into modern European languages, Bruno was, despite a hasty temper, a worthy candidate.

One of his first acts was to crown Otto emperor on 21 May 996. Pope and emperor acted in full harmony, holding a synod that restored Arnulf to Reims and condemned Gerbert, the future Sylvester II, as an intruder. When Otto left Rome, the turbulent noble Crescentius rose and drove Gregory north. Crescentius set up the antipope John XVI, whom Otto's troops later captured, mutilated, and degraded before pope and emperor in 998.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-innocent:
Pope Innocent V, Petrus of Tarentaise, born about 1225, won election at Arezzo 21 January 1276 and died at Rome 22 June 1276, the first Dominican pope. His province was certainly Tarentaise on the upper Isère, his birthplace probably Champagny. He entered the Dominicans at sixteen, took his master of sacred theology at Paris in 1259, and earned renown as a teacher, hailed the most famous doctor.

He led his order in France as provincial, then took Lyons as archbishop in 1272 and Ostia as Cardinal-Bishop in 1273. At Lyons's Second Council in 1274 he gave two sermons and spoke Saint Bonaventure's funeral oration. Gregory X's close adviser, he followed him with a peaceable policy. He made peace between Italy's Guelphs and Ghibellines and between Pisa and Lucca. He brokered between Rudolf of Habsburg and Charles of Anjou and laboured to firm up the Greeks' union with Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-v:
Pope John V, a Syrian, son of Cyriacus, ruled from 685 to 686 and died 2 August 686. As deacon he spoke for the Apostolic See at the Sixth Ecumenical Council. He came back to Rome in July 682 bearing the synod's official papers. Emperor Constantine Pogonatus liked him so well that the emperor cut taxes on papal estates in Sicily and Calabria and lightened the Church's fiscal load overall.

His biographer praises his vigour, learning, and moderation warmly, qualities that no doubt won him election in Saint John Lateran's basilica. Constantine Pogonatus had ended the wait for imperial confirmation, so John went straight to the Lateran palace as pope. Consecration followed about 23 July 685, and his reign ran a little over a year. In that short time he gave 1,900 solidi to clergy and deaconries for the poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-leo-v:
Leo V was a priest from Priapi near Ardea. He served a church outside Rome. He probably held the papacy for about a month in August 903. Lists of the time call him a priest from outside the city. A writer of the time praised his godly life. Almost nothing is known about his election or his reign.

His one recorded act was a bull freeing the canons of Bologna from taxes. Christopher, cardinal-priest of St Damasus, seized him and threw him into prison. There he likely died naturally. One account says Sergius III had both imprisoned popes killed. The entry lays out what can and cannot be known.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-martin-v:
Oddone Colonna was born at Genazzano in 1368. He trained at Perugia. He rose through papal offices. He deserted Gregory XII. He took part in electing antipopes at Pisa. The Council of Constance chose him unanimously on 11 November 1417. He was ordained deacon, priest, and bishop within three days. He was crowned at Constance ten days later.

Martin ended the Western Schism. He won over John XXIII and the successors of Benedict XIII. He struck separate concordats, or agreements, with Germany, France, England, Spain, and probably Italy. Then he set out for a ruined, famine-struck Rome. The entry follows his rebuilding of papal rule. It ends with his death in February 1431.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-nicholas:
Tommaso Parentucelli was born at Sarzana in 1397. His father was a poor physician. Parentucelli lost his father young. He left Bologna unfinished. He tutored Florentine families. He befriended leading humanists. He took a theology degree in 1422. He spent twenty years serving Bishop Albergati of Bologna. He fed a passion for books and building. He shone at the Council of Florence in debate with Greek bishops.

As pope he secured papal rights over bishoprics and benefices. He did so through the Concordat of Vienna in 1448. He won the submission of the last antipope, Felix V. He marked the end of the schism with a great Jubilee in 1450. Plague scattered the pilgrims and drove him from Rome for a time. He returned to receive German princes and prelates. He died there in March 1455.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-paul-v:
Camillo Borghese was born at Rome in 1550. His family came from Siena and claimed St Catherine as a relative. Unrest drove them from Siena to Rome. Camillo studied law at Perugia and Padua, growing into a canonist of marked ability. Clement VIII made him cardinal in 1596, and he became Cardinal-Vicar of Rome.

On Leo XI's death all eyes turned to him, and he took the throne without engagement or obligation. His legal training showed in all he did. He ruled from the decretals, not diplomacy. He held every right claimed by his predecessors inviolate. His first public act sent absentee prelates and cardinals home to their sees. Trent had called episcopal absence a grave sin. He soon fell into controversy with Italian cities over church rights. The entry follows his stern reign to his death in January 1621.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-sixtus-v:
Felice Peretti was born at Grottamare near Montalto in 1521. His Dalmatian family had fled Turkish devastation in Illyria. His father was a gardener, and Felice is said to have herded swine as a boy. At nine he joined Montalto's Minorite convent, where his uncle lived as a friar. He became a novice at twelve and was ordained at Siena in 1547. He won fame as a preacher at Rome in 1552.

Pius IV made him counsellor to the Venetian Inquisition, but his zeal got him recalled in 1560. Elected on 24 April 1585 and crowned on 1 May, he economized ruthlessly except on building. He raised taxes, sold offices, and extended public loans. He built the Lateran Palace, finished the Quirinal, and founded a hospice for the poor. Before his death he had stored three million gold scudi and one million six hundred thousand silver in Sant' Angelo. He died on 27 August 1590.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-pius-:
Michele Ghisleri was born at Bosco near Alessandria in 1504 to a poor but noble family. The Dominicans of Voghera took him in and schooled him in solid, austere devotion. He joined the order, took ordination in 1528, and spent sixteen years teaching theology and philosophy. He served as master of novices and prior of several houses, fasting, doing penance, and spending nights in meditation and prayer.

Paul IV made him bishop of Sutri in 1556, then inquisitor in Milan and Lombardy, and in 1557 cardinal and inquisitor general for all Christendom. At Mondovì from 1559 he restored faith and discipline battered by Piedmont's wars. He blocked Pius IV from admitting thirteen-year-old Ferdinand de' Medici to the Sacred College. He defeated Maximilian II's plan to end clerical celibacy. He was elected on 7 January 1566 and died on 1 May 1572.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-stephen-:
Stephen, son of Marinus, reigned from 816 to 817 and died on 24 January 817. He came from the noble Roman family that gave two other popes to the church. Hadrian I and Leo III patronized his youth; Leo made him deacon. Celebrated for virtue, he won election and consecration at once after Leo's death, about 22 June 816.

At once he made Romans swear allegiance to Louis the Pious as suzerain and notified the emperor of his election. He then travelled to France, crowned Louis, received splendid presents, and renewed the Frankish-papal pact. In Gaul, Theodulf of Orléans, a chief imperial adviser, received the pallium from him. Returning through Ravenna, he displayed Christ's sandals for veneration and brought home exiles banished under Leo III. St Peter's holds his grave.
criticism-part-4-from-the-works-of-john-:
Reviews and short critical pieces by John Greenleaf Whittier fill this file, part four of the Criticism volume, volume seven of his works. Six heads stand in the contents: Evangeline, Mirth and Medicine, Fame and Glory, Fanaticism, The Poetry of the North, and Criticism.

The first piece hails Longfellow's Evangeline as the American poem British critics had long taunted the country for lacking. Whittier praises its scenes from Nova Scotia to the Gulf of Mexico. Fame and Glory takes up an address by Charles Sumner at Amherst College. Other pieces weigh mirth as medicine and the worth of northern verse. The file shows the Quaker poet at work as a working critic of his peers.
doe-osti-17120056-the-arm-aerosol-optica:
Connor Flynn and three Pacific Northwest National Laboratory colleagues document a data product for the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement program. Flynn works at the University of Oklahoma. Report DOE/SC-ARM-TR-211 is dated August 2026. Aerosols, tiny airborne particles, scatter and absorb sunlight. Climate work needs those effects in standard form. The AOP product computes them from raw site instruments.

Inputs come from absorption and scattering instruments at ARM sites. Named correction schemes are applied to the absorption data. Outputs include scattering and absorption coefficients. They also include single scattering albedo. Angstrom exponents describe how effects change with color. Quality checks, file formats, and site coverage are spelled out, so researchers can use the record with confidence.
doe-osti-1763976-helioscope-energy-perfo:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NREL/TP-6A20-78916, issued in February 2026 with Janine Freeman Keith as technical contact, closes out CRADA project CRD-17-00685. The project tested HelioScope, the web-based solar design and performance modeling tool made by Folsom Labs. Banks and cities had hesitated to trust its energy estimates without vetting from a respected laboratory, and Folsom Labs won a Small Business Voucher to get that check done.

HelioScope systems were built with the same specifications and weather-year data used in earlier studies. Its predictions were then compared against measured output from real photovoltaic systems. The same systems were also run through three established tools, the System Advisor Model, PVSyst, and PV*SOL. The comparison shows how closely the newer tool's engine tracks both field data and the older models' results.
doe-osti-2589494-hydrogen-systems-for-pe:
National Renewable Energy Laboratory final report NREL/TP-5D00-96451 closes project CRD-21-21941, called HYPER-V. Technical contact Yiyun Yao, working with partner Eaton, studied hydrogen systems that combine electrolyzers, storage tanks, and fuel cells on the power grid. A hydrogen setup can earn value in several stacked ways, if its controls dispatch it well.

Tasks built and refined simulation models for each device, then joined them into layouts matching real uses. Control software for the electrolyzer, first built under an earlier software record, was matured for dispatch decisions. A market task weighed energy market openings and customer demand shapes to set performance targets. The filing frames when hydrogen systems pay: flexible operation across services, rather than one fixed job.
doe-osti-3003994-versatile-amp-intellige:
Kshitiz Gupta of Lawrence Livermore presents a feasibility study, LLNL-TR-2013728, dated November 2025, for project 25-FS-035. The project, called VIBES, aims at biodetection through environmental sensing. The motivating gap is predictive health monitoring: during the COVID-19 pandemic, testing reacted to illness instead of warning ahead of it. A breath-based sensor could flag both known diseases and new threats.

The project built an optical biosensor that analyzes volatile organic compounds in breath, imitating the sense of smell. Thin metal-coated substrates carried small biological recognition elements. With a visible laser readout, the device detected ethanol reliably down to about 2 parts per million, with early detection of acetone below 100 parts per million. Nanostructures on the film amplified the signal, as expected. Several unexpected influences on sensor behavior were logged for the next design round.
doe-osti-3375873-what-is-produced-water-: Produced water got worth-valued, and this DOE text covers Marcellus Permian. The pages detail the total findings. The energy folks get their data. The proposition was value. The data were energy. The basin were Permian. The Marcellus were formation.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DollahiteVernon:
Patrolman Vernon V. Dollahite of Shelby County was interviewed by the FBI on April 13, 1968. Memphis police and Special Agent Franklin L. Johnson took part. Nine days earlier, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. had been shot at the Lorraine Motel in Memphis, and officers across the area were accounting for their movements.

Dollahite re-enacted what he had done on April 4, the day of the shooting. Interviews of this kind built the investigation's timeline, placing each officer at each hour. His statement preserves one patrolman's part in that record, fixed while memories were still fresh.
in-the-ranks-of-the-c-i-v:
Erskine Childers served as a driver with the City of London Imperial Volunteers battery in South Africa. His diary, In the Ranks of the C.I.V., was published in 1900. He was a clerk in the House of Commons who shipped on the Montfort. Chapters move from Capetown to Bloemfontein and Pretoria.

A shell bursts beside his team and chips his mare's nose in one action. The veldt burns in thin lines of flame as they trot through. Hospital, Warmbad, and the road south close the diary. Childers writes plainly of horses, guns, and daily war work.
king-henry-v:
King Henry V, by William Shakespeare, begins with a Prologue who asks for a muse of fire. He wishes for a kingdom as a stage and princes as actors. Warlike Harry should then appear like Mars, the god of war. Famine, sword, and fire would crouch at his heels for work.

The Prologue admits the small theatre cannot hold the fields of France. He asks the crowd to imagine armies, horses, and Agincourt instead. Two mighty monarchies, he says, are parted by a narrow ocean. Then Canterbury and Ely enter to discuss a bill from the last reign. Their talk turns grand war talk toward church business and law.
leila-or-the-siege-of-granada-book-v:
Book Five of Leila, dated 1838, opens with the great battle. Dawn comes slowly after an awful night. Moors on Granada's battlements watch Ferdinand's whole army march.

The Spanish host moves toward the city walls at last. Wrecks of a blackened camp mark the road of war. Leila's story reaches its crisis amid that assault. Love, faith, and family claims must all be settled. Lytton closes his Granada romance with the fall of Moorish Spain. The Alhambra's fate hangs over every battlefield scene. Lytton ends with loss on the winning side too.
macmillan-s-reading-books-book-v:
Macmillan's Reading Books, Book V, is a school reader for Standard V pupils. Its preface explains the aim of the whole series. The books give a systematic course for schools under state inspection. English rules required fluent reading and seventy-five lines of poetry learned by heart.

The Scotch code asked for three hundred lines of new poetry repeated. Meaning, allusions, and word roots had to be known, not just sounds. Parsing and sentence analysis fill out the higher work. Such readers trained generations of British schoolchildren. They joined good literature to strict grammar drill. Book V shows Victorian schooling at its most earnest and exact.
nasa-tm-19680006060-evaluation-of-direct:
K. E. Demorest and A. F. Whitaker, at the Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama, wrote this memorandum on November 24, 1967. Numbered TM X-53675, it evaluates direct current motors in vacuum. Motors that run happily in air can fail in space, where no air cools them or carries away wear products. Their materials therefore need testing under realistic conditions.

Special materials were chosen for small motors of one-sixth horsepower and worked into the bearing retainers, brushes, and insulation system. The motors then ran in a simulated space environment while component temperatures were monitored. Power output and the torque needed to turn a generator load were recorded throughout. In general, the authors conclude, motor materials are now available that will let direct current motors, open directly to the space environment, operate reliably.
nasa-tm-19700015780-apollo-10-as-505-apo:
Marshall Space Flight Center laboratories prepared this technical summary on May 1, 1969. It covers the Apollo 10 space vehicle, called AS-505, built around the Saturn 5 rocket. Apollo 10 was the dress rehearsal flight for the first Moon landing.

The summary gives a brief, clear description of the whole vehicle. Where needed, it adds related facts to make the picture complete. Where a point needs it, the summary adds related information for clarity. It was not meant to define the vehicle in full detail. Its readers were staff who needed a quick, sound grasp of the craft and its parts before the mission flew.
nasa-tm-19720017951-nasa-balloon-aircraf:
NASA Balloon: Aircraft Ranging, Data and Voice Experiment is a May 1972 report on air traffic control trials. It runs to sixty-nine pages, and its lead author's name is poorly rendered in the scan. High balloons stood in for a satellite during the tests. The concepts under trial were proposed for the ATS-F satellite's planned air traffic control experiment.

The tests ran in September 1971 at Aire-sur-l'Adour in France, with ground stations, balloon platforms, and aircraft supplied by the European Space Research Organization. One ground simulation and two aircraft flights at low elevation angles were conducted at L-band. Even under heavy interference, voice communications and side-tone ranging performed well. The data channels, however, suffered high bit errors that produced false commands, and the report closes with recommendations for improving the equipment.
salem-witchcraft-volumes-i-and-ii-with-a: Charles W. Upham wrote Salem Witchcraft, in Volumes I and II, with an account of Salem Village and a history of opinions on witchcraft and kindred subjects. A note states that the work was originally published in 1867, and the printing shown here is a fourth printing of 1969 from Frederick Ungar Publishing in New York. The contents divide Volume I into a preface, maps and pictures, a general index, an introduction, Part First on Salem Village, and Part Second on witchcraft.
tales-from-many-sources-vol-v:
Tales from Many Sources, Volume V, printed at New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1886, is an anthology of stories gathered from magazines and named authors. Its contents open with Lob Lie-by-the-Fire by Juliana H. Ewing, a tale of the lubber-fiend.

Ewing's introduction explains the creature Lob. He is a rough kind of brownie or house elf. He is said to haunt some north-country homesteads. He does the farm laborers' work overnight. His wages are no grander than a cream bowl duly set. Wild Jack and Out of Season come from Temple Bar, Mr. Josiah Smith's Balloon Voyage from Belgravia, and named tales by Mrs. Forrester, Mary Frances Peard, and A. Mary F. Robinson fill the volume. Such sets carried magazine fiction into book form for family reading.
the-agamemnon-of-aeschylus-translated-in: Aeschylus wrote the Agamemnon. Gilbert Murray rendered it into English rhyming verse. Murray was Regius Professor of Greek at Oxford. His notes support the text. George Allen and Unwin of London printed this tenth-thousand copy. The cast list names Agamemnon first. He is king of Argos and Mycenae. He heads the Greek armies at Troy. His wife Clytemnestra stands next. Her lover Aigisthos follows. Cassandra, Priam's daughter and prophetess, closes the list. She is now Agamemnon's slave.
the-life-and-adventures-of-robinson-crus:
Daniel Defoe novel of Robinson Crusoe of York appears here in volume one of a two volume London edition of 1812. A life of De Foe stands before the tale, matching the biography printed in the 1808 edition record held here. It gives his London birth about 1663 to a butcher father in Cripplegate.

Schooling at Newington, an early pamphlet, and service in the Monmouth rising fill the opening pages. The title page promises Crusoe travels round three parts of the globe, written by himself. Shipwreck, solitude, and Friday wait beyond the long author biography.
the-weavers-a-tale-of-england-and-egypt-:
Gilbert Parker's Weavers continues in this volume record with book two, chapters five to fourteen. A contents list precedes chapter five, The Wider Way, which is built from a letter. Faith Claridge writes from Hamley to her brother David in Cairo, in the Quaker thee-and-thou of their people, asking whether he still loves the village that gave him sour bread.

Faith reports that Jasper Kimber, the man David struck at the public-house, followed a lass to London and begged her to marry him. She refused, then relented conditionally: three years sober and hard-working would earn him an answer. Kimber, laid up with fever, opened his whole mind to Faith and grew thankful for David's knocks. The letter mixes reproach, gossip, and forgiveness.
un-doc-united-nations-special-committee-:
Chapter V of the 1947 report of the United Nations Special Committee on Palestine weighs what could be done about the land's future. UNSCOP had toured Palestine and heard Jews and Arabs state rival claims. Britain was ending its mandate, and a choice could not be put off.

The chapter tests the main options against the facts the panel had gathered. It looks at partition, a single shared state, and other plans for rule. It sets out the gains and costs of each path. This groundwork leads straight to the rival plans that close the report.
